Disorders of the Eye Special Senses — Neurology Unit

Glaucoma

LO 1–6
2nd leading cause of blindness worldwide Open-angle vs. Angle-closure ~65M affected globally

Glaucoma is a group of optic neuropathies defined by characteristic optic disc and visual field changes — not simply by elevated intraocular pressure (IOP), which is a major risk factor but neither necessary nor sufficient for the diagnosis. The two major forms, open-angle and angle-closure, differ almost completely in tempo, symptoms, and mechanism, which is exactly what exam questions like to test.

🎓 What Boards Would Say

Boards almost never open with the word "glaucoma" — they hand you a stem and expect the exam-cue pattern-match to happen before the diagnosis is ever named. Here's roughly how each form gets introduced:

Open-angle stem

"A 68-year-old man of African descent presents to his primary care physician for a routine annual physical. He has a history of hypertension and has not seen an eye doctor in over five years. He reports no visual complaints and denies eye pain, redness, or headache. On further questioning, he admits he has been bumping into furniture on his left side more often lately. Visual acuity is 20/25 in both eyes. Intraocular pressure is 26 mmHg in the right eye and 24 mmHg in the left. Fundoscopic examination reveals a cup-to-disc ratio of 0.7 bilaterally with thinning of the neuroretinal rim. Visual field testing shows peripheral field loss in both eyes. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?"

Answer: Primary open-angle glaucoma

Angle-closure stem

"A 62-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with severe pain in her right eye, headache, nausea, and vomiting that began two hours ago while she was watching a movie in a dark theater. She describes seeing halos around lights. On examination, the right eye is red with a hazy, edematous cornea and a fixed, mid-dilated pupil. Intraocular pressure is 54 mmHg in the right eye and 16 mmHg in the left. The left eye examination is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?"

Answer: Acute angle-closure glaucoma — an ophthalmologic emergency

▶
▶ Glaucoma | Clinical Presentation
Video — "Glaucoma | Clinical Presentation" (YouTube)
Natural History
Epidemiology
  • Second leading cause of blindness worldwide — an estimated 65 million people affected (~3.5% global prevalence)
  • Primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) is the most common form overall; highest prevalence in populations of African descent
  • Angle-closure glaucoma is comparatively rare but presents acutely; highest prevalence in populations of Asian descent
  • Affects roughly 1–2% of the U.S. population
Risk factors
  • Hypertension
  • Family history of glaucoma
  • Race — African ancestry (open-angle), Asian ancestry (angle-closure)
  • Age > 50 years

Untreated, both forms progress to irreversible optic nerve damage: open-angle does so silently over years, while an acute angle-closure attack can cause severe, permanent loss within hours to days.

Pathophysiology

Aqueous humor is produced by the nonpigmented ciliary epithelium, flows from the posterior chamber through the pupil into the anterior chamber, and drains mainly through the trabecular meshwork into the canal of Schlemm, with a smaller uveoscleral outflow route as well. Glaucoma results whenever outflow can no longer keep pace with production, regardless of which step fails.

Open-angle
↑ Trabecular meshwork resistance
→
Outflow impeded despite an open angle
→
Chronic IOP elevation
→
Progressive RGC / optic nerve loss

Primary (gene mutation) or secondary — usually associated with another ocular disease.

Angle-closure
Mechanical obstruction of the outflow pathway
→
Acute IOP spike
→
Rapid optic nerve damage

Can be precipitated by an enlarging lens (e.g. a maturing cataract) pushing the lens–iris diaphragm forward — phacomorphic angle closure.

Secondary open-angle mechanisms — pseudoexfoliation (PEX) material and pigment shed from the back of the iris (pigment dispersion syndrome) both clog the trabecular meshwork and raise outflow resistance
Clinical Presentation
Open-angle
  • Insidious onset, slowly progressive
  • Painless peripheral visual field loss — "tunnel vision" late in disease
  • Typically bilateral
  • IOP often elevated, but can be only high-normal
Angle-closure
  • Acute onset, painful red eye
  • Field loss progresses periphery → fovea
  • Often with headache, nausea, vomiting
  • Typically unilateral, can be bilateral
Red flag — refer urgently

An acute painful red eye with headache and nausea/vomiting should raise concern for acute angle-closure glaucoma — an ophthalmologic emergency requiring same-day IOP-lowering treatment and referral.

Diagnostic Workup
Finding / TestSignificance
Cup-to-disc ratioA ratio > 0.5, or notable asymmetry between eyes, is suggestive of glaucomatous optic neuropathy
Intraocular pressure (tonometry)Elevated IOP supports the diagnosis, but normal-tension glaucoma exists — IOP alone can't rule glaucoma in or out
Visual field perimetryDetects and stages the characteristic peripheral field defects

Differential diagnosis

  • Physiologic cupping of the optic disc
  • Congenital optic disc anomalies
  • Ischemic optic neuropathy (e.g. compressive tumor)
  • Trauma (closed-head injury)
  • Hereditary optic neuropathies
Treatment
Pharmacologic

Every class works by one of two levers:

↓ Aqueous production
·
↑ Aqueous outflow
  • Topical β-blockers — ↓ aqueous production
  • Topical α-agonists — ↓ production, mild ↑ outflow
  • Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (topical or oral) — ↓ production
  • Prostaglandin analogues — ↑ uveoscleral outflow; often first-line
  • Cholinergic agonists (e.g. pilocarpine) — ↑ trabecular outflow via ciliary muscle contraction / miosis
Laser / Surgical
  • Selective laser trabeculoplasty (SLT) — improves trabecular outflow

The LiGHT trial found a single SLT treatment brought ~75% of eyes to target IOP with no topical medication needed — supporting SLT as a reasonable first-line option, not just a fallback after drops fail.

Mechanism of action — glaucoma medications

PGF2α analogues

e.g. latanoprost

  • ↓ outflow resistance of the trabecular meshwork
  • ↑ uveoscleral outflow by relaxing the ciliary muscle and disrupting turnover of extracellular matrix
β-blockers

e.g. timolol

  • Diminish aqueous humor production by inhibiting Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase
α2 agonists

e.g. brimonidine

  • ↓ episcleral venous pressure
  • Diminish aqueous humor production by inhibiting Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase
Cholinomimetics

e.g. pilocarpine

  • Widen the trabecular meshwork via ciliary muscle activation
  • Open the iridocorneal angle by activating the iris sphincter muscle (miosis)
Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors

e.g. acetazolamide

  • Diminish aqueous humor production
Rho-kinase inhibitors

e.g. netarsudil

  • ↑ trabecular outflow
  • ↓ episcleral venous pressure
  • ↓ aqueous humor production by increasing noradrenergic transmission
Mechanism of action — where each drug class acts on aqueous humor production (ciliary epithelium) vs. outflow (trabecular meshwork, uveoscleral pathway, episcleral venous pressure)
Monitoring & Complications
  • Serial IOP checks and visual field perimetry to confirm treatment is halting progression
  • Watch for topical medication adverse effects — local irritation, and systemic effects from absorbed β-blockers (e.g. bradycardia, bronchospasm)
  • Vision loss from glaucoma is irreversible — treatment aims to preserve remaining vision, not restore what's already lost
Prevention & Health Promotion

Regular eye screening — particularly for patients over 50, those with a family history, or those with ancestry-linked risk (African descent for open-angle, Asian descent for angle-closure) — is the main prevention strategy, since open-angle glaucoma is frequently asymptomatic until significant, irreversible field loss has already occurred.

🔑 Pearl

Don't anchor on IOP alone: open-angle glaucoma can present with a normal or high-normal pressure, and the diagnosis rests on optic disc and visual-field changes. Angle-closure, by contrast, is the one that announces itself — sudden, painful, and usually unilateral.

Cataracts

LO 1–4
Leading cause of blindness worldwide ~70% prevalence > 80 y/o Surgery is the only definitive treatment

A cataract is an opacity of the crystalline lens. The overwhelming majority are acquired and age-related, developing slowly and painlessly; a much smaller congenital subset presents in infancy and is a true time-sensitive diagnosis, since a delayed diagnosis risks irreversible deprivation amblyopia. No drug reverses lens clouding — the entirety of definitive treatment is surgical.

🎓 What Boards Would Say

Two very different stems, two very different urgencies — one you counsel and schedule, one you refer today.

Age-related stem

"A 72-year-old woman presents with several months of progressively blurry vision. She reports that the blurring is worse when driving at night, with significant glare and halos around oncoming headlights. She also mentions that she recently stopped needing her reading glasses, which she found surprising. She denies eye pain, redness, or discharge. Visual acuity is 20/50 in both eyes. Fundoscopic examination reveals a diminished red reflex bilaterally. Slit-lamp examination shows a yellow-brown, cloudy discoloration of the central lens in both eyes. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?"

Answer: Age-related (nuclear) cataract

Congenital stem

"A 6-week-old female infant is brought in by her mother for a routine well-child visit. The mother reports that the infant does not seem to track faces or objects as well as her older sibling did at this age. On examination, red reflex testing reveals a white pupillary reflex in the left eye; the right eye's red reflex is normal. The infant is otherwise healthy, feeding well, and meeting other developmental milestones. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?"

Answer: Urgent referral to pediatric ophthalmology (congenital cataract) — leukocoria also requires retinoblastoma to be ruled out

▶
▶ CATARACT, Causes, Signs and Symptoms, Diagnosis and Treatment
Video — "CATARACT, Causes, Signs and Symptoms, Diagnosis and Treatment" (YouTube)
Natural History
Epidemiology
  • Leading cause of visual impairment and blindness worldwide
  • Prevalence rises steeply with age: ~17.5% at 40–80 y/o, ~70% by > 80 y/o
  • Sex: ♀ > ♂
Etiology
  • Age-related (> 90% of acquired cases) — by far the most common cause
  • Secondary to ocular/systemic disease ("complicated cataract") — diabetes mellitus, renal insufficiency/dialysis, Wilson disease, retinitis pigmentosa, acute glaucoma, prior retinal detachment, chronic uveitis
  • Drug-induced — glucocorticoids (local or systemic), miotics (cholinesterase inhibitors)
  • Chronic alcohol and tobacco use
  • Traumatic — contusion or perforation injury, intraocular infection
  • Physical — ionizing/UVB radiation, high-voltage current or lightning, infrared exposure ("glassblower's cataract")
  • Congenital (< 1%) — TORCH infections (esp. rubella), galactosemia, hypocalcemic tetany, myotonic dystrophy, trisomy 21/13/18, Alport syndrome, neurofibromatosis type 2, Marfan syndrome

Left untreated, cataracts progress toward complete blindness. Congenital cataracts carry an additional, time-sensitive risk: if not corrected early, the brain permanently suppresses input from the affected eye — irreversible deprivation amblyopia.

Pathophysiology
Lens dehydration + oxidative damage
→
Low-MW protein breakdown products aggregate into high-MW clumps
→
Altered refractive index, light scattering
→
Progressive lens opacification

Three morphologic types, distinguished by where in the lens the opacity starts:

Nuclear
  • Central lens, yellow-brown discoloration
  • Most common age-related pattern
Cortical
  • Outer layer, wedge-shaped ("spoke") opacities growing inward
  • More common in diabetes
Posterior subcapsular
  • Just under the posterior capsule; granular deposits
  • Younger patients — steroid use, diabetes, trauma; progresses fastest
Classification — cortical (spokes), nuclear sclerosis (central opacity), and posterior subcapsular (granule deposits) patterns, with a mature cataract for comparison
Slit-lamp — posterior subcapsular cataract, fine granular deposits just under the posterior capsule

Progression is also staged by severity: immature (red reflex still present) → mature (red reflex absent; white-yellow lens) → hypermature/Morgagnian (liquefied cortex, brown nucleus sinks within it).

Clinical Presentation
Acquired cataract
  • Reduced visual acuity — blurred, clouded, or dim vision, worse at night
  • Painless, often bilateral
  • Glare and halos — from daylight, low sun, or oncoming headlights
  • "Second sight" — a temporary improvement in near vision from a myopic shift, classically with nuclear cataracts
  • Monocular diplopia or polyopia — resolves when the affected eye is covered
  • Diminished or altered color perception
Congenital cataract
  • Leukocoria — white pupillary reflex, often first caught on newborn red reflex screening
  • Strabismus, nystagmus
  • Delayed motor skill development
  • Deprivation amblyopia if uncorrected
Congenital cataract — infant eye exam (lid speculum), dilated pupil with cloudy white opacification of the lens nucleus
Red flag — refer urgently

Leukocoria on a newborn or infant red reflex exam needs prompt referral to pediatric ophthalmology. Every week of delay increases the risk of permanent deprivation amblyopia — and leukocoria also needs retinoblastoma ruled out.

Diagnostic Workup
Finding / TestSignificance
Visual acuityMay be normal early; progressively decreases as the cataract advances. Cortical cataracts can manifest as a hyperopic shift.
Fundoscopy / red reflexDiminished or absent red reflex, leukocoria, or obscured fundus detail depending on density
Slit-lamp examGrey, white, yellow, or brown clouding of the lens, pattern depending on type; traumatic cataract classically shows rosette/stellate-shaped clouding

Differential diagnosis

  • Age-related macular degeneration
  • Diabetic retinopathy
  • Glaucoma
Mature cataract — diffuse white opacification, absent red reflex
Typical appearance — cloudy, yellow-tinged lens on slit-lamp exam
Traumatic (contusion) cataract — rosette/stellate-shaped clouding on retroillumination
Treatment

No pharmacologic agents treat cataracts — surgery is the only definitive management. Congenital cataracts should be operated on as soon as possible to prevent deprivation amblyopia.

Indications
  • Significant visual impairment from the cataract (most common reason)
  • Marked interocular difference in refractive power
  • Cataract obstructing exam/treatment of posterior structures (e.g. the fundus)
  • Cataract causing glaucoma (e.g. phacomorphic angle closure)
Contraindications
  • Visual disturbance manageable with corrective lenses
  • Vision not expected to improve (e.g. concurrent ocular pathology)
  • High surgical risk

Surgical options

TechniqueCharacteristics
PhacoemulsificationLiquefies/aspirates the nucleus through a small, sutureless incision; IOL placed in the posterior chamber. Best visual outcomes and lowest complication rate of the options here, but highest cost and may not suit very advanced cataracts.
Extracapsular cataract extraction (ECCE)Nucleus removed via anterior capsulotomy, posterior capsule retained, IOL in posterior chamber. More cost-efficient than phaco; often needs suture removal.
Intracapsular cataract extraction (ICCE)Entire lens (incl. posterior capsule) removed; IOL placed in the anterior chamber or sutured to the iris. Largely obsolete — larger incision, slower healing, higher complication rate (e.g. postsurgical astigmatism).
Manual small incision cataract surgery (MSICS)Lens removed through a small incision, can be sutureless. Similar visual outcomes to phaco at lower cost.
🔑 Pearl

A hypermature (Morgagnian) cataract with deposits in the anterior chamber is a clue that lens proteins are leaking out and triggering a macrophage response — phacolytic glaucoma. Same underlying lens, but now it's an emergency, not just a vision problem.

Macular Degeneration

LO 1–4
Leading cause of blindness > 65y in developed countries Dry ~90% vs. Wet ~10% Central vision only

Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is a degenerative disease of the central retina (macula) that spares peripheral vision — the opposite pattern from open-angle glaucoma, which is exactly why boards likes to pair them. Dry AMD (~90%) is driven by drusen deposition and progresses over decades; wet AMD (~10%) is driven by choroidal neovascularization and can progress over weeks. Both are painless, but wet AMD is the one that can't wait.

🎓 What Boards Would Say

The tempo of the stem is the whole diagnosis here — slow and gradual vs. sudden and distorted.

Dry AMD stem

"A 78-year-old man presents with gradual worsening of his central vision over the past several years. He has difficulty reading fine print and recognizing faces of people across the room, but he has had no trouble navigating around furniture or walking outside. He denies eye pain or redness. Visual acuity is 20/70 in both eyes. Amsler grid testing reveals mild distortion of the grid lines. Fundoscopic examination reveals numerous small, round, yellow-white deposits scattered throughout the macula bilaterally, without hemorrhage or exudate. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?"

Answer: Dry (nonexudative) age-related macular degeneration

Wet AMD stem

"A 74-year-old woman presents with a one-week history of distorted vision in her right eye. She states that the lines on her kitchen tile now appear wavy and bent. She denies any pain. Amsler grid testing confirms significant metamorphopsia in the right eye. Fundoscopic examination of the right eye reveals a grayish-green elevation of the macula with a surrounding area of subretinal hemorrhage. The left eye examination is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?"

Answer: Urgent referral for wet (neovascular) AMD — intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy is time-sensitive

▶
▶ Macular Degeneration
Video — "Macular Degeneration" (YouTube)
Natural History
Epidemiology
  • Leading cause of blindness in individuals > 65 years in developed countries
  • Usual age of onset > 55 years; prevalence rises steeply with age — from ~0.2% at 55–64 y/o to ~13.1% at > 84 y/o
  • Sex: ♀ > ♂; more prevalent in White populations
Etiology
  • Multifactorial — metabolic, functional, genetic, and environmental factors
  • Strong genetic component; complement pathway genes are implicated
  • Risk factors: advanced age, family history/genetic predisposition, cardiovascular disease, smoking, obesity

Both forms follow a chronic, progressive course. Dry AMD has a significantly better prognosis than wet AMD, and complete loss of central vision is possible but rare in either.

Pathophysiology

Both forms converge on progressive degeneration of the central retina → visual impairment, but the mechanism and tempo diverge completely.

Dry AMD (~90%)

Nonexudative / atrophic AMD

Drusen (lipid + vitronectin + protein) deposit under the RPE / between RPE and Bruch membrane
→
Slow, progressive atrophy of the RPE

Four contributing processes: lipofuscinogenesis, drusogenesis, inflammation, and (in advanced disease) neovascularization — advanced dry AMD can progress to geographic atrophy or convert to wet AMD.

Wet AMD (~10%)

Exudative / neovascular AMD

VEGF-driven choroidal neovascularization between RPE and Bruch membrane
→
Leakage of serous fluid / blood
→
Sudden macular elevation ± RPE detachment

Considered an advanced form of AMD; VEGFA is a key driver of the neovascularization.

Normal retina vs. dry AMD (drusen, atrophic RPE) vs. wet AMD (neovascularization, hemorrhage, fluid leakage) — microscopic anatomy and corresponding fundoscopy
Clinical Presentation
Dry AMD
  • Slow, progressive visual impairment, usually over decades
  • Unilateral or bilateral onset
Wet AMD
  • Acute or insidious onset — over weeks to months
  • Usually manifests in one eye first

Shared features

  • Painless central or pericentral visual impairment — reduced visual acuity, difficulty adapting to changes in lighting
  • Metamorphopsia — straight lines appear wavy; tested with an Amsler grid
  • Scotoma (blind spot)
Red flag — don't sit on this one

New or rapidly worsening metamorphopsia, especially with acute vision change, should raise concern for wet AMD. Anti-VEGF therapy works best started early, so this warrants prompt ophthalmology referral rather than routine follow-up.

Diagnostic Workup
Finding / TestSignificance
Amsler gridDetects metamorphopsia and scotomas — quick screening/monitoring tool for either form
Fundoscopy — dry AMDDrusen, retinal pigment epithelium atrophy, RPE hypertrophy (mottling)
Fundoscopy — wet AMDGrayish-green retinal discoloration, serous detachment of the retina/RPE, subretinal or intraretinal hemorrhage/exudate, fibrous disciform scars
Fluorescein angiographyDry AMD: well-defined hyperfluorescence of the altered RPE. Wet AMD: diffuse hyperfluorescence from neovascularization and exudation — helps confirm wet AMD
Optical coherence tomography (OCT)Detects intra-/subretinal fluid; confirms wet AMD diagnosis and monitors treatment response

Differential diagnosis

  • Open-angle glaucoma — insidious, but peripheral vision loss instead of central
  • Central retinal artery occlusion — acute, complete vision loss, swollen disc
  • Retinal detachment — acute, "falling curtain" vision loss
  • Cataract — insidious, blurred/dim vision and glare, absent or opacified red reflex
Drusen — yellow subretinal deposits in the macula and along the temporal vascular arcade
Dry AMD — dense, confluent drusen with RPE mottling, no hemorrhage or neovascularization
Dry AMD — extensive drusen with RPE hyperpigmentation surrounding the disc
Treatment

No causal treatment exists for either form — management is supportive for dry AMD and targeted at neovascularization for wet AMD.

Supportive (both forms)
  • Patient education
  • Visual/reading aids — e.g. magnifying glass
  • Risk-factor avoidance (e.g. smoking cessation)
  • Diet rich in green leafy vegetables and fish
  • Antioxidant therapy — vitamins A, C, E, beta-carotene, zinc
Wet AMD — targeted
  • First-line: intravitreal anti-VEGF injection (ranibizumab, bevacizumab, pegaptanib)
  • Second-line (if anti-VEGF contraindicated):
    • Laser coagulation — direct thermal coagulation of the neovascularization
    • Photodynamic therapy — IV dye activated by laser light → local toxicity → thrombosis of the subretinal neovascularization
🔑 Pearl

AMD spares peripheral vision and hits central vision — glaucoma does the opposite. If a stem gives you central scotoma + metamorphopsia, think macula (AMD); if it gives you tunnel vision, think optic nerve (glaucoma).

Diabetic Retinopathy

LO 1–4
Leading cause of blindness, ages 20–74 NPDR → PDR → complications Early detection prevents ~90% of blindness

Diabetic retinopathy is a retinal microangiopathy that is usually silent until it isn't — most cases are picked up on a routine screening exam, not because the patient noticed anything wrong. It progresses along a predictable track: nonproliferative changes (leaky vessels) → proliferative changes (neovascularization), with macular edema able to complicate either stage. That track is exactly what boards expects you to know.

🎓 What Boards Would Say

One version of this stem is a quiet screening finding; the other is a phone call from the ED.

NPDR stem

"A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus of 12 years' duration presents for his annual diabetic eye examination. He reports no visual complaints and states that his vision feels normal. His hemoglobin A1c is 8.9%. Dilated fundoscopic examination reveals scattered microaneurysms, dot-and-blot hemorrhages, and hard exudates in both eyes. There is no evidence of neovascularization. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?"

Answer: Nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR)

PDR stem

"A 34-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes mellitus of 18 years' duration presents to the emergency department with sudden, painless loss of vision and new floaters in her right eye that began this morning. She was diagnosed with proliferative diabetic retinopathy one year ago and missed her last two follow-up appointments. Fundoscopic examination of the right eye is significantly limited due to a poor view of the fundus. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her vision loss?"

Answer: Vitreous hemorrhage complicating proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR)

▶
▶ Diabetic Retinopathy | Endocrine System Diseases | NCLEX-RN | Khan Academy
Video — "Diabetic retinopathy | Endocrine system diseases | NCLEX-RN" (Khan Academy, YouTube)
Natural History
Epidemiology
  • Most common cause of visual impairment and blindness in patients aged 20–74 years
  • Type 1 DM: ~80% develop retinopathy after 15 years
  • Type 2 DM (> 30 y/o): not requiring insulin — ~25% by 5 years, ~50% by 19 years. Requiring insulin — ~40% by 5 years, ~85% by 19 years
  • Poorly controlled long-term diabetics: ~60% develop some retinopathy by 15–20 years; with intensive metabolic control, only ~20% do by 20 years
  • Worldwide diabetes prevalence is projected to reach 429 million by 2030 — as many as 10 million could develop visual complications
Etiology / risk factors
  • Poor glycemic control — HbA1c is the best predictor of development and progression
  • Increased duration of diabetes; presence of diabetic nephropathy
  • Hypertension, dyslipidemia
  • Puberty, pregnancy
  • History of cataract surgery
  • Other modifiable factors: sleep apnea, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, serum prolactin/adiponectin/homocysteine levels

Early detection and treatment can prevent up to 90% of diabetic retinopathy-related blindness. Left unaddressed, disease progresses from silent microvascular change to vision-threatening complications — macular edema, vitreous hemorrhage, tractional retinal detachment, and neovascular glaucoma.

Pathophysiology

Both vascular and neural retinal tissue are affected — loss of retinal supporting cells, basement membrane thickening, and altered retinal blood flow set up two parallel downstream problems: leaky vessels and hypoxia.

Chronic hyperglycemia → retinal capillary microangiopathy
→
Leaky, damaged capillaries
→
Hemorrhage, hard exudates, edema
Retinal ischemia
→
Nerve fiber layer infarcts ("cotton-wool spots")
→
VEGF-driven neovascularization
→
Fibrovascular proliferation, traction on the retina

Three overlapping patterns, distinguished by mechanism and findings:

NPDR

Microangiopathy → leaking vessels → retinal hemorrhages

PDR

Chronic hypoxia → abnormal vessel proliferation → traction on the retina → retinal detachment

Diabetic macular edema

Leaking vessels → lipid/fluid infiltration → macular edema. Can complicate NPDR or PDR at any stage.

Normal retina vs. diabetic retinopathy — hemorrhage, microaneurysm, cotton-wool spots, hard exudates, and abnormal (neovascular) blood vessel growth
Clinical Presentation
  • Early stages are usually asymptomatic — most cases are found on routine screening, not patient complaint
  • Symptoms, when present, usually reflect a complication (macular edema, vitreous hemorrhage, retinal detachment):
    • Blurred vision
    • Floaters
    • Photopsia
    • Scotoma
    • Sudden, painless vision loss
  • Later stages: significant visual impairment progressing to blindness
Red flag — refer urgently

New floaters, photopsia, or sudden painless vision loss in a patient with known or long-standing diabetes should raise concern for a proliferative complication — vitreous hemorrhage or tractional retinal detachment — and warrants urgent ophthalmology referral, not routine follow-up.

Diagnostic Workup
Finding / TestSignificance
Screening — dilated eye exam or retinal photographyHow most diabetic retinopathy is actually found. Start within 5 years of diagnosis for T1DM; at diagnosis for T2DM. Annual interval (every 2 years may be reasonable if the initial exam is normal and glycemic control is good).
NPDR findingsMicroaneurysms, venous caliber changes, intraretinal hemorrhage, hard exudates, retinal edema, cotton-wool spots, intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMA)
PDR findingsNPDR findings plus neovascularization (the hallmark) → fibrovascular proliferation → vitreous hemorrhage, traction retinal detachment; rubeosis iridis → secondary (neovascular) glaucoma
Diabetic macular edemaClinically significant retinal thickening/edema involving the macula, with associated hard exudates — can occur at any stage of NPDR or PDR
Optical coherence tomography (OCT)Cross-sectional retinal imaging; used to assess for and follow macular edema
Fluorescein angiographyFurther characterizes severity and identifies neovascularization/other complications
Fundus photo — hard exudates (scattered yellow dots), microaneurysms (small vessel bulges), and small hemorrhages (blurry red dots)
Treatment

Every patient: refer to ophthalmology, optimize glycemic control, manage ASCVD risk factors (treat hypertension, initiate lipid-lowering therapy as indicated, continue aspirin if indicated for another reason), and arrange regular follow-up eye exams — screen for other microvascular complications too, given the high rate of co-occurrence.

NPDR
  • Mild–moderate: observation only; reassess every 6–12 months
  • Severe: treat as PDR — PRP and/or anti-VEGF
PDR
  • Panretinal photocoagulation (PRP) and/or anti-VEGF — roughly equally effective
  • PRP often preferred first-line (single session, lower risk of loss to follow-up)
  • Anti-VEGF alone reasonable for motivated patients with reliable follow-up
Diabetic macular edema
  • Center-involving: first-line intravitreal anti-VEGF; PRP or focal/grid laser depending on severity
  • Non-center-involving: PRP, anti-VEGF, or focal/grid laser depending on severity

Refractory disease or severe complications (e.g. tractional retinal detachment, vitreous hemorrhage) → vitrectomy.

Adjunct pharmacologic therapy

  • Renin-angiotensin system inhibitors — reduce complications in type 1 DM
  • PPAR-α agonists — reduce risk of retinal complications
  • Glucocorticoids — reduce retinal inflammation and edema
🔑 Pearl

Diabetic retinopathy is asymptomatic until it isn't — that's precisely why annual screening is standard of care for every diabetic, not an optional extra. Early detection and treatment can prevent up to 90% of the blindness this disease would otherwise cause.
